newsitem.title: USA: Calif. offshore oil faces challenge from Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Calif. offshore oil faces challenge from Mexico.

text.p: Prices for California's offshore crudes could slip to historic lows this summer as competition from a Mexican import heats up after a six-year absence, market observers said.
Los Angeles refiners this summer are again buying Maya crude -- a viscous, high-sulphur grade long considered too toxic for most facilities to process economically.
But record rates of production have allowed Mexico's Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) to drop Maya's price and persuaded Los Angeles refiners to run the grade for the first time since 1991.
Maya, with a relatively heavy API gravity of 22 degrees, and high sulphur content of four percent, is nearly the same as California's Outer Continental Shelf (OSC) crudes.
"It's definitely going to pressure (down) OCS," said a trader for a major California oil company.
Pemex has also eliminated an environmental roadblock to exports by agreeing to remove hydrogen sulphide from the grade in Mexico, market players said.

Traders said Maya, which loads on Mexico's Pacific coast, is selling for a discount of $3.20 (fob) under an average of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude, and California's heavy Kern River grade.

The discount comes on top of a 18 percent drop in the average price of Maya crude this spring from a year earlier as Maya crude output rose 10 percent over the same period. The icnreased production is part of a Mexican program to boost crude exports, specifically Maya, in the next four years.

Already, reduced prices have lured five California refiners to take delivery of nearly 1.7 million barrels of Maya in July and August, traders said, presenting serious competition to OCS's 125,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) production.
Pemex has not confirmed the shipments, but has said it was in negotiations with several West Coast refineries to export Maya.
Texaco, which has a small stake in OSC along with major holders Exxon and Chevron, says OCS has always competed well with foreign grades, and will continue to do so.
